processing: Pan-fired and pressed flat, the classic Long Jing method: heat in the wok stops oxidation and gives the blade-like leaf and its bean-like aroma.
harvest_season: Spring. As with West Lake Long Jing generally, leaf picked around Qingming (about 5 April) as one bud and one leaf ranks highest.
appearance_dry: Flat, smooth blades with the yellowish 'brown rice' tone this zone is known for, rather than a bright green.
appearance_wet: As with other fine Long Jing, tender buds and single leaves, soft and fresh green.
taste_profile: A pure aroma of beans and fresh grass over a gentle sweetness, with the clean, soft finish expected of top Long Jing.

brewing.notes: Use a glass or a gaiwan left open. Water around 80 °C keeps the sweetness; hotter water brings out the bitterness quickly.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, with the pre-Qingming and Qingming pickings at the top of the price range. It is a tea to drink fresh, usually within a year. The name is a place claim that is hard to verify, so a seller's account of the plot and picking date matters.
description:
Shi Feng Long Jing is West Lake Long Jing from the Lion Peak zone above Hangzhou, centred on Shizi Feng and taking in Hugong Temple, Longjing village, Shang Tianzhu and Qipan Shan. Yangmeiling village also counts it as a main local product. In the traditional ranking of West Lake zones it sits at the top.

It is made like any Long Jing, fired in a wok and pressed flat. What marks it out is colour and aroma: a yellowish 'brown rice' tint instead of vivid green, and a pure scent that is the point of the tea.

Expect beans and fresh grass with a soft sweetness, strongest in the first two steeps. The usual mistake is water that is too hot or leaf left to stew, which turns a delicate cup flat and bitter.

Buy by season and by trust. A very bright green leaf is not what this zone is prized for, and because Shi Feng is the most famous name in Long Jing it is widely attached to tea from elsewhere. Tasting it beside a Long Jing from another West Lake zone, such as Weng Jia Shan, is the fastest way to learn the difference.
history:
West Lake Long Jing served as a tribute tea in earlier times, and its zones came to be ranked by name. The Lion zone, Shi Feng, was singled out as the finest, with its leaf described by its pure aroma and brown-rice colour.

No single person or date is credited with the Shi Feng name. Today it works as a mark of place within West Lake Long Jing rather than a separate kind of tea.
